title: Persistent Demo-Pool Poisoning Attacks on Online LLM Log Parsers

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to identify a new security vulnerability in online LLM log parsers that use self-generated in-context learning (SG-ICL). No prior paper explicitly identifies vulnerabilities specific to SG-ICL systems in the context of log parsing. Papers [3] and [4] discuss vulnerabilities in in-context learning (ICL) broadly, including poisoning attacks, but neither focuses on SG-ICL systems or log parsing. Paper [15] identifies vulnerabilities in log parsers but does not address SG-ICL or self-generated demonstrations. Thus, no prior paper establishes the same empirical relationship.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves showing that the monotonically growing, never-purged demonstration pool of SG-ICL systems creates a persistent attack surface that adversaries can corrupt via crafted log injection. Paper [3] introduces ICLPoison, which demonstrates that ICL systems are vulnerable to data poisoning attacks, and paper [4] discusses poisoning the demonstration context in ICL systems. Both papers describe mechanisms for corrupting ICL systems via adversarial manipulation of the demonstration pool, which is substantively equivalent to the mechanism described here, even though SG-ICL is not explicitly mentioned.

### Evaluation
The evaluation is conceptual identification grounded in AdaParser's design, where entries are never purged or revalidated. Papers [3] and [4] use similar conceptual evaluations to identify vulnerabilities in ICL systems, relying on the design properties of ICL (e.g., reliance on demonstration context). Paper [15] also uses conceptual identification to highlight vulnerabilities in log parsers. These prior papers employ the same evaluation design — identifying vulnerabilities based on system design properties — making the evaluation facet covered.

### Domain
The domain is AIOps/LLM-based log parsing security. Papers [1], [5], [7], [8], [9], [10], and [11] all address LLM-based log parsing, which is the same general application area. While none of these papers focus on security vulnerabilities, the domain facet is judged at the area level, not the specific sub-problem. Therefore, the domain is covered.
